sections.text:
1 Catal., I, p. 130, 26 ss.
2 Cf. infra p. 234, 7.
3 Bar-Hebraeus, l. c., El Qifti, infra p. 231, n. 2.
4 Hist. Dyn. ed. Pococke, p. 147.
5 Paulo aliter historia narratur in Bar-Hebraei Chronico syriaco (ed. Bedjan,
p. 127, 4 ss.), cuius versionem gallicam comiter mihi misit vir humanissimus Rubens
Duval. Qua textus arabicus vel potius interpretatio Pocockii optime illustratur :
Théophile servait le calife Al-Mahdi, qui l'estimait beaucoup à cause de sa supério-
rité dans l'art de l'astrologie. On raconte que certain jour le calife voulut se rendre
dans une de ses provinces et emmener sa cour avec lui. L'épouse du calife envoya
dire à Théophile : “ C'est toi qui a conseillé au calife ce voyage et nous a imposé la
fatigue et l'ennui de la route dont nous n'avions nul besoin. J'espère donc que Dieu
te fera périr et disparaître de ce monde afin que débarrassées de toi nous trouvions du
repos. „ Théophile répondit à la servante qui lui avait porté ce message : “ Retourne
vers la maîtresse et dis-lui : ce n'est pas moi qui ai conseillé au roi ce voyage; il
voyage quand il lui plaît. Quant à la malédiction que tu as lancée contre moi pour
que Dieu accélère ma mort, la décision en a déjà été prise et affirmée par Dieu : je
mourrai prochainement ; mais ne t'imagine pas que je mourrai parce que ta prière
aura été exaucée : c'est la volonté de mon créateur qui s'accomplira. Mais toi, ô
reine, je te dis : prépare pour toi beaucoup de poussière, et quand tu apprendras que
je suis mort, amoncelle toute cette poussière sur ta tête. „ Lorsque la reine eut
entendu ces paroles, elle fut saisie d'une grande frayeur, et elle attendit quel serait
le résultat. Peu après Théophile mourut et vingt jours après le calife Al-Mahdi
mourut également. Ce que Théophile avait déterminé se réalisa donc.
sections.en:
1 Catal., I, p. 130, 26 ff.
2 Cf. below p. 234, 7.
3 Bar-Hebraeus, loc. cit., El Qifti, below p. 231, n. 2.
4 Hist. Dyn. ed. Pococke, p. 147.
5 The story is told slightly differently in Bar-Hebraeus's Syriac Chronicle (ed. Bedjan,
p. 127, 4 ff.), a French version of which the most humane man Rubens
Duval kindly sent me. By which the Arabic text or rather Pococke's interpretation is excellently illustrated:
Theophilus served the caliph Al-Mahdi, who esteemed him highly because of his superio-
rity in the art of astrology. It is said that one day the caliph wanted to go
to one of his provinces and take his court with him. The caliph's wife sent
word to Theophilus: “It is you who advised the caliph on this journey and imposed on us the
fatigue and boredom of the road which we had no need of. I hope therefore that God
will make you perish and disappear from this world so that rid of you we may find some
rest.” Theophilus replied to the servant who had brought him this message: “Return
to the mistress and tell her: it is not I who advised the king on this journey; he
travels when it pleases him. As for the curse you have launched against me so
that God may hasten my death, the decision has already been taken and affirmed by God: I
shall die soon; but do not imagine that I shall die because your prayer
will have been answered: it is the will of my creator which will be accomplished. But you, O
queen, I tell you: prepare for yourself much dust, and when you learn that
I am dead, heap all this dust on your head.” When the queen had
heard these words, she was seized with a great fright, and she waited to see what would be
the result. Shortly after Theophilus died and twenty days later the caliph Al-Mahdi
died also. What Theophilus had determined was therefore realized.

summary.headline: Theophilus and Caliph Al-Mahdi
summary.text: Biography of Theophilus, son of Thomas, a Christian astrologer from Edessa who became chief astrologer to Caliph Al-Mahdi after serving on a campaign through Margiana. The page recounts his prediction of Al-Mahdi’s death twenty days after his own, with references to Bar Hebraeus and related Arabic and Syriac accounts.
